content: Fairbanks disease, also known as multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED), is a rare genetic disorder that primarily affects the growth and development of the ends of bones, known as epiphyses. This condition occurs in approximately 1 in 10,000 births and is most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, although an autosomal recessive form also exists. In normal bone growth, cartilage is deposited at the ends of bones in a process called ossification, which eventually mineralizes and hardens into bone. In individuals with MED, this ossification process is defective, leading to abnormalities in bone development. The disorder represents a spectrum of skeletal abnormalities, with varying degrees of severity. Children with the autosomal dominant form of MED typically experience joint pain and fatigue, particularly after physical activity. Radiographic imaging often reveals small, irregular ossification centers, most notably in the hips and knees. A waddling gait may develop over time. The spine is generally normal, though minor irregularities may be present. By adulthood, individuals with this form of MED are usually of short stature or at the lower end of the normal height range, with disproportionately short limbs compared to their trunk. Joint mobility may become restricted, especially in major joints such as the elbows, although hypermobility can occur in the knees and fingers. Early-onset osteoarthritis is a common complication, often beginning in early adulthood. In the autosomal recessive form of MED, affected children also experience joint pain, particularly in the hips and knees. However, this form is often associated with additional skeletal deformities, such as abnormalities of the hands, feet, knees, or spine (e.g., scoliosis). Approximately 50% of children with the recessive form exhibit noticeable abnormalities at birth, such as clubfoot, cleft palate, inward-curving fingers due to underdeveloped bones, or, in rare cases, swelling of the ears. During childhood, height is typically within the normal range, but as adults, individuals with this form of MED may have slightly reduced stature, though still within the normal range. Functional joint disabilities are generally mild or absent in this form of the disease.
